# Sulphonamide drugs (`sulphonamides`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/medicine.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Medicine & hygiene (`medicine`)
- Deps: needs synthetic_dyes, contagion_theory; helped by controlled_trial, microorganisms
- Core idea: Prontosil is a red dye that the body converts to sulphanilamide, a colourless compound. That conversion explains why the drug protected animals despite disappointing early tests in glass dishes. Sulphonamides interfere with bacterial folate synthesis and can arrest the growth of susceptible bacteria. Early successes included treatment of streptococcal childbed fever; later compounds extended the range of treatable infections. Activity depends on the organism and resistance. Kidney injury, severe allergic reactions and unsafe formulations all limited use.
- Pitfalls:
  - Screening candidate drugs only in the test tube; Prontosil does nothing there and works in the animal
  - Believing it is the dye colour that kills germs
  - Dissolving the drug in an untested solvent: the American 'Elixir Sulfanilamide' of 1937, made with diethylene glycol, killed over 100 people
  - Expecting every member of the drug class to treat the same infections, or using an antibacterial drug for a viral illness
  - Short or low dosing, which bred resistant gonorrhoea within a few years
- History: europe: 1908 – Gelmo (Vienna) synthesises sulphanilamide as a dye intermediate; 1932 Domagk at Bayer finds Prontosil protects mice (published 1935); 1935 Jacques and Thérèse Tréfouël, Nitti and Bovet (Paris) show sulphanilamide is the active part; 1936 Colebrook's trial in childbed fever; 1938 sulphapyridine (M&B 693); americas: 1937 – Elixir Sulfanilamide disaster leads to the US Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act of 1938
- Read:
  - Gerhard Domagk, Ein Beitrag zur Chemotherapie der bakteriellen Infektionen, Deutsche medizinische Wochenschrift (1935)
  - John E. Lesch, The First Miracle Drugs: How the Sulfa Drugs Transformed Medicine (2007)
  - Thomas Hager, The Demon Under the Microscope (2006)
